name: Agrarian socialism
scope: The agrarian socialism of the Russian Socialist Revolutionaries (Narodnik heirs; Chernov's land socialization, peasantry and industrial workers as one toiling class, democratic and peaceful land reform), as the scholarship and Britannica define it (s1, s2, s3); the Saskatchewan CCF farmer-socialism that Lipset's study calls agrarian socialism (s4); and the Oklahoma Socialists' farmer programme against tenancy, crop liens and usury (s5, which cites Bissett's Agrarian Socialists in America). It excludes state-collectivization regimes (Maoist China, Khmer Rouge, North Korea): none of these defining sources files them under the label. Texts count only as far as these sources tie them to it; the Regina Manifesto is not tied by any source that names the label, so it is not cited.

summary: Agrarian socialism seeks to end large private landholding and give land to those who work it, as personal, family or cooperative labour ownership, while treating peasants as part of one toiling class with industrial workers. Its best-documented strand, the Russian Socialist Revolutionaries, paired land socialization with a democratic state, acceptance of industrial modernity and, before 1917, terrorism against the Old Regime.
